placeholders.name: GRADE
placeholders.what: The grade level and, if relevant, the course track of the class you're planning for. You'll find this on your class roster or master schedule. A good value is specific, like '7th grade' or '10th grade Algebra 1'; a bad value is vague like 'middle school.'
examples: 7th grade
10th grade (Algebra 1, general track)
3rd grade (self-contained classroom)

placeholders.name: SUBJECT
placeholders.what: The subject area of the lesson, matching how you'd describe it on your schedule or gradebook. Be specific enough to signal the discipline's conventions, since a science lesson and a writing lesson need very different activity types.
examples: U.S. History
Physical Science
English Language Arts - persuasive writing

placeholders.name: MINUTES
placeholders.what: The number of minutes in this specific class period today, written as one plain number. Check your bell schedule, since block days or shortened schedules change this from a normal day. A bad value is a range like '45-50' — give one number so the AI can build a plan that actually adds up.
examples: 90 (block schedule)

placeholders.name: PASTE STANDARD
placeholders.what: The exact wording of the standard or objective you're teaching to, copied from your state standards document, curriculum guide, or district pacing guide — not paraphrased from memory. Getting the exact wording matters because the AI builds every activity around what this specific sentence actually requires students to do.
examples: CCSS.ELA-LITERACY.RI.7.8: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient.
NGSS MS-PS1-4: Develop a model that predicts and describes changes in particle motion, temperature, and state of a pure substance when thermal energy is added or removed.
State standard 8.G.A.1: Verify experimentally the properties of rotations, reflections, and translations.

placeholders.name: PRIOR KNOWLEDGE
placeholders.what: A short, honest description of what students have already learned or practiced that's relevant to today's lesson, including any recent gaps. Think back over your last week or two of lessons, not the whole year. A bad value is 'they know the basics' — that tells the AI nothing about where to start the hook.
examples: Students can identify claims and evidence in a text but haven't practiced evaluating whether the evidence is sufficient. We covered claim vs. counterclaim last week.
Students know the particle model of matter at a basic level (solid/liquid/gas) from 6th grade but have never connected it to energy transfer.
Students can plot points and reflect shapes over the x-axis; rotations are brand new content today.

placeholders.name: MATERIALS, e.g. "whiteboard, Chromebooks, no printer access"
placeholders.what: What's physically available in your classroom today, including anything that's normally available but isn't today, like a broken printer or a Chromebook cart being used by another class. This keeps every activity in the plan realistic instead of asking students to use a device or handout you don't actually have.
examples: Whiteboard, projector, 1 Chromebook per student, no printer access today
Textbooks, poster paper, markers, no technology available
Interactive whiteboard, lab stations with basic equipment, printed handouts allowed

variations.label: Emergency Sub Plan
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you'll be absent and a substitute with no background in your content needs to run the entire class alone, so every step must be spelled out with no assumed classroom routines.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me write a lesson plan detailed enough for a substitute teacher who does not know my students, my routines, or this subject to run alone.

CONTEXT
Grade level: [GRADE]
Subject: [SUBJECT]
Class length: [MINUTES] minutes
Standard/objective (exact wording): [PASTE STANDARD]
What students already know: [PRIOR KNOWLEDGE]
Materials available today: [MATERIALS, e.g. "whiteboard, Chromebooks, no printer access"]
Classroom routines the sub should know: [ROUTINES, e.g. "students get a warning then move seats if disruptive; bathroom pass is on the hook by the door"]

Build a lesson plan with these sections, each with a time allotment that adds up to [MINUTES] minutes:
1. Hook/warm-up — include the EXACT words the sub should say out loud to start it.
2. Direct instruction — write it as a script the sub can read aloud, not just bullet points, since they don't know this content.
3. Guided practice — a task the sub does WITH the class, with the exact instructions to give.
4. Independent practice — a task students do alone or in pairs, with exact written instructions to put on the board.
5. Formative check — a simple way for the sub to collect evidence of who understood it, that doesn't require subject expertise to evaluate.
6. What to do if a section runs short or long — give the sub a one-line backup for each.

Rules: Do not invent facts about my school, students, or curriculum beyond what I gave you. Assume the sub has zero familiarity with this subject and cannot answer content questions, so the plan must be self-contained.

variations.label: Multi-Day Lesson Arc
variations.whenToUse: Use this when one class period isn't enough to cover the standard properly and you need the objective spread across 2-3 connected class periods instead of forced into a single day.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me plan a short unit arc that spreads one objective across multiple class periods.

CONTEXT
Grade level: [GRADE]
Subject: [SUBJECT]
Number of days: [NUMBER OF DAYS, e.g. "3"]
Class length per day: [MINUTES] minutes
Standard/objective (exact wording): [PASTE STANDARD]
What students already know: [PRIOR KNOWLEDGE]
Materials available: [MATERIALS, e.g. "whiteboard, Chromebooks, no printer access"]

For EACH day, build a lesson plan with these sections, each with a time allotment that adds up to [MINUTES] minutes:
1. Hook/warm-up (connect to the previous day if it's not day 1)
2. Direct instruction
3. Guided practice
4. Independent practice
5. Formative check
6. Homework/extension (optional, one line)

Across the days, make sure the cognitive demand builds — day 1 shouldn't just repeat day 2's content at a lower level — and tell me, in one line per day, what evidence would tell me a student is ready to move to the next day's content versus needs to stay on the current one.

Rules: Do not invent facts about my school, students, or curriculum beyond what I gave you. If the objective doesn't realistically fit in the number of days I gave you, tell me what to cut or which day to add, instead of quietly compressing it.

variations.label: Co-Teach / Small Group Split Version
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you have a co-teacher, aide, or paraprofessional in the room and want the plan to specify who leads which part and how the class splits into groups.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me plan a single class lesson that I will teach alongside a co-teacher/aide.

CONTEXT
Grade level: [GRADE]
Subject: [SUBJECT]
Class length: [MINUTES] minutes
Standard/objective (exact wording): [PASTE STANDARD]
What students already know: [PRIOR KNOWLEDGE]
Materials available today: [MATERIALS, e.g. "whiteboard, Chromebooks, no printer access"]
Second adult in the room and their role: [CO-TEACHER ROLE, e.g. "special education co-teacher, can pull a small group of 5 students"]

Build a lesson plan with these sections, each with a time allotment that adds up to [MINUTES] minutes, and for each section note which adult leads it and what the other adult is doing at the same time:
1. Hook/warm-up
2. Direct instruction
3. Guided practice
4. Independent practice, split into a whole-class group and a small pulled-out group
5. Formative check — one version for the whole class, one adapted version for the small group
6. Homework/extension (optional, one line)

Rules: Do not invent facts about my school, students, or curriculum beyond what I gave you. If the sections don't realistically fit in [MINUTES] minutes, tell me what to cut instead of quietly keeping everything.

followUps.label: Tighten unrealistic timing
followUps.prompt: Be honest with me: which of these six sections is most likely to run long in a real classroom, and why? Rebuild the time breakdown assuming that section takes 3-5 minutes longer, and tell me exactly what to cut to still end on time.

followUps.label: Add differentiation for this lesson
followUps.prompt: Add one sentence to the guided and independent practice sections describing a quick adjustment for students who are struggling and one for students who finish early, without changing the core objective or timing.

followUps.label: Make the formative check faster to grade
followUps.prompt: The formative check you gave me takes too long to collect and grade before the bell. Give me a version that takes under 2 minutes to administer and under 5 minutes total to skim for who needs a follow-up.

followUps.label: Script the hook word-for-word
followUps.prompt: Write out the exact words I should say to open the hook/warm-up, as if I'm reading a script, including the question I ask students and one example of a strong versus weak student response.

tch-b1-lesson-plan-from-objectives.walkthrough:
Dana Ruiz teaches 7th grade U.S. History and has 45 minutes tomorrow to cover causes of the American Revolution before a unit test on Friday. She opens Claude and pastes the lesson-plan prompt, filling in GRADE as "7th grade," SUBJECT as "U.S. History," MINUTES as "45," PASTE STANDARD as her state's standard about analyzing multiple causes of the Revolution, PRIOR KNOWLEDGE as "students read a short article on the Stamp Act last week but haven't connected multiple causes together yet," and MATERIALS as "whiteboard, projector, 1 Chromebook per student, no printer access today."

Claude returns a six-part plan: a 5-minute hook where students rank three grievances by "how angry would this make you," 12 minutes of direct instruction on four causes (taxation, representation, quartering, trade restrictions), a 10-minute guided practice sorting activity done as a class, a 12-minute independent practice where pairs pick one cause and write two sentences connecting it to an event, a 4-minute exit ticket asking students to name one cause and rate their confidence 1-3, and a one-line homework extension. The times add to exactly 45.

Dana notices the guided practice sounds vague about what actually goes on the board, so she sends the follow-up asking Claude to script the hook word-for-word and, since she wants the guided part clearer too, asks it to lay out the sorting activity as an exact board layout with two filled-in example rows. Claude responds with the opening question read aloud, plus a four-column table she can copy directly onto the whiteboard.

Total time: about 9 minutes, including typing in her details and one follow-up. She now has a full lesson plan, a script for the opening minute, and a ready-to-use board layout for tomorrow morning.

placeholders.name: OBJECTIVE
placeholders.what: The single learning objective that all three versions must still teach, written as a clear 'students will be able to...' statement — copy this from your lesson plan or standard. A good value is specific and measurable; a bad value is vague like 'understand photosynthesis.'
examples: Students will explain how cells convert glucose and oxygen into usable energy (ATP) and identify the byproducts of that process.
Students will identify the author's main argument in a persuasive text and evaluate whether two pieces of evidence are relevant and sufficient.
Students will solve one-step linear equations involving addition and subtraction and check their solution by substitution.

placeholders.name: PASTE READING OR WORKSHEET
placeholders.what: The full original text of the reading or worksheet you want tiered, pasted in completely, including any existing questions. Don't summarize it — if you paste a thin summary instead of the real document, the AI will have to invent details to fill the gaps, which breaks the rule about not inventing content.
examples:
Cellular respiration is the process cells use to convert glucose and oxygen into usable energy called ATP. This process happens mainly in an organelle called the mitochondria. During cellular respiration, glucose reacts with oxygen, producing carbon dioxide, water, and ATP as byproducts. Plants and animals both perform cellular respiration, even though plants also perform photosynthesis. Without enough oxygen, cells can only produce a small amount of ATP through a less efficient backup process.

Questions:
1. What two byproducts are produced during cellular respiration besides ATP?
2. Where in the cell does most cellular respiration occur?
3. Why can't cells produce as much ATP without oxygen?

Some people think school should start later for teenagers. Studies show teenagers naturally stay up later and need more sleep than adults think. When schools start too early, students are tired and don't learn as well. Later start times could mean better grades and safer driving for teens who drive themselves to school. Critics say a later start time would mess up after-school sports and parents' work schedules.

Questions:
1. What is the author's main argument?
2. What is one piece of evidence the author gives to support it?

variations.label: Two Tiers Only
variations.whenToUse: Use this when your class doesn't have students who need an extension challenge, or you only have time to prep two versions instead of three.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me differentiate a classroom material into two versions that both teach the SAME objective at different levels of accessibility.

OBJECTIVE (must stay identical across all versions): [OBJECTIVE]
ORIGINAL MATERIAL: [PASTE READING OR WORKSHEET]

Create two versions:
1. SUPPORT: for students who need scaffolding — add vocabulary definitions and sentence starters, simplify sentence structure, but keep the core concept and required thinking intact. Do not remove the objective's cognitive demand, only the language barrier.
2. ON-LEVEL: lightly cleaned-up version of the original, usable by the rest of the class.

Both versions must be answerable using the same answer key logic (equivalent questions, adjusted wording). List the answer key once and note where wording differs per tier. Do not invent content that isn't grounded in the original material or the stated objective.

variations.label: Add an ELL Layer
variations.whenToUse: Use this when a meaningful number of your students are English language learners and need a fourth version with visual supports and cognates, not just simplified English.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me differentiate a classroom material into four versions that all teach the SAME objective at different levels of accessibility, including one designed for English language learners.

OBJECTIVE (must stay identical across all versions): [OBJECTIVE]
ORIGINAL MATERIAL: [PASTE READING OR WORKSHEET]
HOME LANGUAGES IN MY CLASS: [HOME LANGUAGES, e.g. "Spanish and Haitian Creole"]

Create four versions:
1. SUPPORT: for students who need scaffolding in English — add vocabulary definitions and sentence starters, simplify sentence structure, but keep the core concept and required thinking intact.
2. ELL: same simplifications as SUPPORT, plus flag cognates with the home languages listed where they exist, suggest where a visual or diagram would replace a text-heavy sentence, and keep sentences under 12 words where possible.
3. ON-LEVEL: lightly cleaned-up version of the original.
4. EXTENSION: same objective, but add a layer of complexity, ambiguity, or an extra analytical step for students ready to go further.

All four versions must be answerable using the same answer key logic (equivalent questions, adjusted wording). List the answer key once and note where wording differs per tier. Do not invent content that isn't grounded in the original material or the stated objective, and do not guess at translations you aren't confident in — flag them for me to verify instead.

variations.label: Differentiate a Test Instead of a Worksheet
variations.whenToUse: Use this for a formal graded assessment rather than a practice worksheet, where point values must stay exactly equivalent across tiers for grading fairness.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me differentiate a graded test into three versions that all assess the SAME objective at different levels of accessibility, while keeping scoring fair and equivalent.

OBJECTIVE (must stay identical across all versions): [OBJECTIVE]
ORIGINAL TEST: [PASTE READING OR WORKSHEET]
TOTAL POINTS THE TEST MUST BE WORTH: [TOTAL POINTS, e.g. "20"]

Create three versions, each worth exactly [TOTAL POINTS] points distributed the same way across questions:
1. SUPPORT: for students who need scaffolding — add vocabulary definitions and sentence starters, simplify sentence structure, but keep the required thinking and point value per question intact.
2. ON-LEVEL: lightly cleaned-up version of the original.
3. EXTENSION: same objective and point total, but add a layer of complexity or an extra analytical step for students ready to go further.

All three versions must be gradable with the same answer key logic (equivalent correct answers, adjusted wording) and the same point value per equivalent question, so a Support-tier student and an Extension-tier student who both fully demonstrate mastery earn the same total score. List the answer key once with points per question, and note where wording differs per tier. Do not invent content that isn't grounded in the original material or the stated objective.

followUps.label: Check the reading level actually dropped
followUps.prompt: Look at the SUPPORT version again and tell me its approximate reading grade level compared to the original. If it's not meaningfully simpler, revise it further — shorten sentences and add more vocabulary support — without cutting any of the required thinking.

followUps.label: Verify the answer key truly matches across tiers
followUps.prompt: Go through each question in all three versions side by side and confirm the correct answer is genuinely equivalent, not just similarly worded. Flag any question where a wording change in Support or Extension could accidentally change what counts as correct.

followUps.label: Make the extension meaningfully harder
followUps.prompt: The EXTENSION version feels too close to the on-level version. Add a genuine extra layer — an ambiguous case, a comparison to a related concept, or a 'justify your answer' component — so it's clearly a step up in cognitive demand, not just longer.

followUps.label: Add a student self-check
followUps.prompt: Add one short self-check box at the end of each version — 2-3 questions students can use to judge whether they're ready to move up a tier next time, phrased in plain student-facing language.

tch-b2-differentiated-materials.walkthrough:
Marcus Webb teaches 9th grade Biology and has a one-page reading on cellular respiration that's too dense for about a third of his class, while another third finishes early every time. He opens Claude, fills OBJECTIVE with "Students will explain how cells convert glucose and oxygen into usable energy (ATP) and identify the byproducts of that process," and pastes the full reading, six sentences plus three original questions, into PASTE READING OR WORKSHEET.

Claude returns three labeled versions. The Support version breaks long sentences into two, defines "mitochondria" and "ATP" in a side box, and adds sentence starters like "Cellular respiration happens in the ___ because ___." The On-Level version tightens the original wording without changing content. The Extension version keeps the same three questions but adds a fourth asking students to compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration and defend which is more efficient for a sprinting muscle cell. Claude also lists one shared answer key with a note: "Extension Q4 has no single correct answer — grade on reasoning quality, not a fixed answer."

Marcus reads the Support version and feels the sentences are still a bit long for his lowest readers, so he sends the follow-up asking Claude to check the reading level drop and simplify further while keeping every science term intact. Claude shortens several sentences and adds one more visual cue: "Look for the word ENERGY — that's your clue."

Total time: about 8 minutes from pasting the reading to having three print-ready versions with a shared answer key, which Marcus copies into three separate Google Docs for the next day's class.

placeholders.name: PASTE FULL SOURCE TEXT
placeholders.what: The complete text you actually taught from — a textbook excerpt, article, or your own notes — pasted in full. The AI is instructed to only use facts present here, so if you paste a thin summary instead of the real material, it won't have enough content to write a fair, well-grounded quiz.
examples: The water cycle describes how water moves through Earth's systems in four main stages. Evaporation occurs when the sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, turning it into water vapor that rises into the atmosphere. Condensation happens when that water vapor cools and forms clouds. Precipitation occurs when water falls back to Earth as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. Collection happens when precipitation gathers in oceans, lakes, rivers, and underground reservoirs called aquifers, where the cycle begins again. Plants also release water vapor into the air through a process called transpiration, which contributes to the evaporation stage.

The Silk Road was a network of trade routes connecting China to the Mediterranean Sea, active from around 130 BCE to the 1450s CE. Merchants carried silk, spices, and precious metals westward, while gold, ivory, and glassware moved eastward. Beyond goods, the Silk Road spread ideas, religions such as Buddhism, and technologies including papermaking. Caravans relied on oasis cities like Samarkand and Kashgar for water and rest. The route declined after the rise of sea trade routes in the 15th century made ocean shipping faster and cheaper.

variations.label: Quick 5-Question Exit Ticket
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you need a fast formative check at the end of class instead of a full graded quiz.
variations.prompt:
You are creating a 5-question exit ticket based ONLY on the source material below. Do not add facts, dates, or details that are not present in this source.

SOURCE MATERIAL: [PASTE FULL SOURCE TEXT]

Build 5 questions students can answer in under 5 minutes: 2 multiple choice (4 options each), 2 true/false where any false statement requires the student to also write the correction, and 1 short answer.

For every question, provide the correct answer and a one-line justification citing the specific sentence or fact in the source that supports it. If you are unsure whether a question is fully supported by the source, flag it instead of guessing.

variations.label: Higher-Order Thinking Version
variations.whenToUse: Use this for advanced students or an honors section, when you want questions that go beyond recall into application and analysis.
variations.prompt:
You are creating a quiz based ONLY on the source material below, but focused on application and analysis rather than recall. Do not add facts, dates, or details that are not present in this source, and do not ask students to use outside knowledge beyond what's here.

SOURCE MATERIAL: [PASTE FULL SOURCE TEXT]

Build an 8-question quiz where every question requires students to apply, compare, or analyze the source rather than just recall a fact from it — for example, predicting what would happen if a described process were interrupted, or comparing two things mentioned in the source. Use a mix of short answer and extended response.

For every question, provide a model answer and a one-line justification citing the specific sentence or fact in the source it's grounded in. Assign a point value to each question. If you're unsure whether a question can be fully answered using only this source, flag it instead of guessing.

variations.label: Multi-Source Synthesis Version
variations.whenToUse: Use this when the quiz should draw from two or more source texts you taught together and you want students to compare or connect them, not just recall each separately.
variations.prompt:
You are creating a quiz based ONLY on the source materials below. Do not add facts, dates, or details that are not present in these sources.

SOURCE MATERIAL 1: [PASTE FULL SOURCE TEXT]
SOURCE MATERIAL 2: [PASTE SECOND SOURCE TEXT]

Build a 10-question quiz: 3 questions testing Source 1 only, 3 questions testing Source 2 only, and 4 questions requiring students to compare or connect information across both sources.

For every question, provide the correct answer and a one-line justification citing which source and specific sentence or fact supports it. Assign a point value to each question. If you are unsure whether a question is fully supported by the sources, flag it instead of guessing.

followUps.label: Resolve flagged questions
followUps.prompt: For every question you flagged as unsure or not fully supported, either rewrite it so it's clearly grounded in the source I gave you, or tell me exactly what one sentence I'd need to add to my source material to make it fair to ask.

followUps.label: Format for import into Google Forms
followUps.prompt: Reformat this quiz as a simple list I can paste into Google Forms — one line per question, options lettered A-D on separate lines for multiple choice, and the correct answer marked clearly at the end of each question instead of in a separate answer key.

followUps.label: Even out the difficulty
followUps.prompt: Look at the 10 questions and tell me which ones are genuinely easy, medium, and hard. If most of them cluster at one difficulty level, rewrite 2-3 questions so the quiz has a better spread across easy, medium, and hard.

followUps.label: Add short-answer grading guidance
followUps.prompt: For the 3 short-answer questions, write a brief rubric for each — what a full-credit answer must include, and what a partial-credit answer looks like — so I can grade them consistently and quickly.

tch-b3-quiz-assessment-generation.walkthrough:
Priya Anand teaches 6th grade Science and just finished a two-day unit on the water cycle using a textbook section and her own slide notes. She wants a quiz for Friday but doesn't want to write ten questions from scratch. She opens Gemini, pastes her combined source material, the textbook section on evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection, plus her extra notes on groundwater, into PASTE FULL SOURCE TEXT, and sends the quiz-generation prompt as written.

Gemini returns 10 questions: four multiple choice, each with a wrong-answer explanation like "Option B, sublimation, is plausible because it also involves a state change, but it's not covered as a step in this cycle," three short answer, and three true/false where two of the three false statements require a written correction. Each question lists a point value, and one short-answer question is flagged: "Not confident this is fully supported — the source mentions runoff but doesn't explain how it differs from infiltration. Consider removing or adding a sentence to your source."

Priya reads the flag, realizes she never actually explained infiltration in class, and sends the follow-up asking Gemini to resolve the flagged question by rewriting it so it's grounded in what she actually taught. Gemini replaces it with a question about condensation that cites the exact sentence in her notes.

Total time: about 9 minutes, including pasting her notes and one round of follow-up. She copies the finished quiz into Google Forms for Friday, confident every question traces back to something she actually taught.

placeholders.name: ASSIGNMENT TYPE
placeholders.what: The kind of work you're giving feedback on, described in plain terms — e.g. 'argumentative essay,' 'lab report,' 'math problem set.' This shapes the tone and vocabulary of the comment, so be specific rather than just typing 'assignment.'
examples: argumentative essay on social media regulation
chemistry lab report on reaction rates
unit 3 fractions problem set

placeholders.name: PASTE
placeholders.what: This placeholder appears twice in the prompt: once after 'RUBRIC/CRITERIA,' where you paste your actual grading rubric or the criteria you scored against, and once after 'MY SHORTHAND NOTES AND SCORES,' where you paste your own quick grading notes and the score you gave. Fill each occurrence with the content that matches its label — don't reuse the same text for both.
examples: Rubric (4 categories, 4 points each): 1) Claim clarity — specific, arguable thesis. 2) Evidence use — at least 2 credible sources, correctly cited. 3) Counterargument — addresses an opposing view. 4) Mechanics — grammar, spelling, sentence variety.

Shorthand notes: Score 13/16. Claim is clear but buried in paragraph 2, not the intro. Used the Pew Research stat well; second source was misquoted. No counterargument paragraph. A few comma splices in paragraphs 3-4.
Shorthand notes: Score 7/10. Strong opening thesis. Cited only 1 of the 2 required sources. Counterargument present but only one sentence, not developed. Clean mechanics, no errors found.

placeholders.name: PASTE 1-3 EXAMPLES
placeholders.what: One to three short direct quotes copied word-for-word from the student's actual paper, not your summary of what they wrote. These let the AI reference real language in the feedback instead of writing something generic. Pick quotes that clearly show the strength or the problem you noted.
examples: "Congress should regulate social media because it's obviously bad for kids and everyone knows it."
"According to a 2023 Pew Research study, 46% of teens say they are online almost constantly, which shows how deeply integrated social media has become in daily life."
"Some people might disagree, but I still think social media should be regulated." (only sentence addressing an opposing view)

placeholders.name: GRADE
placeholders.what: The grade level of the student whose work you're giving feedback on. This shapes vocabulary and tone — feedback for a 4th grader reads differently than feedback for an AP senior. Use the actual grade you teach, not a general range.
examples: 10th grade
6th grade
AP-level 11th grade

variations.label: Batch Mode for a Whole Class Set
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you're grading 25+ papers in one sitting and want a faster, repeatable process instead of running the full prompt separately for each student.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me write feedback comments for multiple students' [ASSIGNMENT TYPE] at once, using the same rubric.

RUBRIC/CRITERIA: [PASTE]
STUDENT GRADE LEVEL: [GRADE]

I will give you one student at a time in this format:
Student: [name or ID]
Notes and score: [shorthand notes]
Quote(s): [1-3 quotes]

For each student, write a feedback comment (120-180 words) with this structure: one specific strength referencing their actual quote, one specific area to improve referencing my notes and describing the pattern, and one concrete next step. Use only what I give you for that student — do not carry over details from a previous student or invent anything. Wait for me to paste each student before writing their comment. Match a warm but honest teacher tone appropriate for [GRADE]-level students.

variations.label: ELL / Emerging Writer Version
variations.whenToUse: Use this for an English language learner or emerging writer where the feedback needs to acknowledge language-acquisition progress separately from content mastery, with gentler, more scaffolded next steps.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me write a feedback comment for an English language learner's [ASSIGNMENT TYPE].

RUBRIC/CRITERIA: [PASTE]
MY SHORTHAND NOTES AND SCORES: [PASTE]
SPECIFIC QUOTES OR EXAMPLES FROM THEIR WORK: [PASTE 1-3 EXAMPLES]
STUDENT GRADE LEVEL: [GRADE]
ENGLISH PROFICIENCY LEVEL: [PROFICIENCY LEVEL, e.g. "WIDA Level 3, intermediate"]

Write a feedback comment (120-180 words) with this structure:
1. One specific content strength AND one specific language-growth strength, each referencing the actual quote or example I gave you.
2. One specific area to improve, focused on the single highest-priority pattern rather than a long list of every error, described gently.
3. One concrete, doable next step written in short, simple sentences.

Rules: Use only the strengths, weaknesses, and quotes I gave you. Do not invent examples from the student's work that I did not provide. Keep language simple enough for the student to read the comment themselves, and keep the tone encouraging — this student is still building English proficiency, not just content mastery.

variations.label: Peer-Feedback Training Version
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you want a model comment to show students what strong peer feedback looks like, rather than a comment you'll give directly to one student.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me create a MODEL feedback comment to teach my class what strong peer feedback looks like, based on one real (anonymized) student example.

RUBRIC/CRITERIA: [PASTE]
MY SHORTHAND NOTES AND SCORES: [PASTE]
SPECIFIC QUOTES OR EXAMPLES FROM THE WORK: [PASTE 1-3 EXAMPLES]
STUDENT GRADE LEVEL: [GRADE]

Write a feedback comment (120-180 words) with this structure: one specific strength referencing the actual quote, one specific area to improve describing the pattern, and one concrete next step. Then add a short 'What makes this good feedback' breakdown (3 bullet points) I can show students, explaining why it references specific evidence instead of general praise, why it names a pattern instead of just a mistake, and why the next step is doable.

Rules: Use only what I gave you — do not invent examples from the student's work. Remove any identifying details so this is safe to share with the class as an anonymized model. Keep the tone appropriate for [GRADE]-level students.

followUps.label: Make it sound more like me
followUps.prompt: This reads a little generic and AI-polished. Rewrite it in a more conversational, slightly informal teacher voice — the kind I'd actually say out loud to a student — while keeping the same structure and only the details I gave you.

followUps.label: Shorten it
followUps.prompt: This is too long for a student or parent to actually read closely. Cut it down to 100-120 words while keeping the specific quote, the pattern, and the one next step intact.

followUps.label: Double-check no invented details
followUps.prompt: Reread the comment and flag anything in it that isn't directly traceable to the rubric, notes, or quotes I gave you. I need to be sure nothing about this student's work was invented or assumed.

followUps.label: Adjust the tone for this specific student
followUps.prompt: This student has been discouraged lately and needs a gentler opening. Keep the same strength, area to improve, and next step, but rewrite the opening sentence to feel more encouraging before it gets into feedback.

tch-i1-feedback-comments.walkthrough:
Elena Cho teaches 10th grade English and just finished grading a stack of argumentative essays. She wants better comments than "good job, work on transitions" but doesn't have time to write each one from scratch. She opens Claude, sets ASSIGNMENT TYPE to "argumentative essay on social media regulation," pastes her rubric criteria (four categories: claim clarity, evidence use, counterargument, mechanics) into the first PASTE, pastes her shorthand grading notes, "claim clear but buried in paragraph 2; used one source well, second source misquoted; no counterargument; a few comma splices," into the second PASTE, and pastes two direct quotes from the essay into PASTE 1-3 EXAMPLES, including one where the student wrote "Congress should regulate because it's obviously bad for kids."

Claude writes a 150-word comment. It opens by praising the specific move of using a real source, naming the quote, names the pattern of asserting claims like "obviously bad" without evidence, and gives one concrete next step: "before you submit, highlight every sentence with 'obviously' or 'clearly' and replace it with a specific fact or statistic."

Elena thinks the opening reads a little clinical for this particular student, who has been discouraged lately, so she sends the follow-up asking Claude to adjust the tone and warm up the opening line while keeping the rest the same. Claude revises the opening to acknowledge the student's improvement since the last essay.

Total time: about 6 minutes per student once she has her rubric and notes ready, versus the 12-15 minutes she used to spend writing comments from scratch.

9th grade Algebra 1
Kindergarten

variations.label: Add a Language-Access Layer

variations.prompt:
You are helping me draft parent communication templates for a [GRADE] classroom, written so they translate cleanly for families who use a translation app.

Write templates for these scenarios: [LIST SCENARIOS, e.g. 1) missing homework pattern (repeat), 2) positive recognition, 3) grade concern check-in, 4) unexcused absence follow-up]

For each template:

- Use a warm, professional, non-alarmist tone even for concerns.

- End every concern-type message with a collaborative next step (a call, a meeting, or a specific ask) — never just a complaint.

Do not include specific grades, names, or incidents — these are reusable templates, not messages about a real student yet.
