tch-i2-parent-communication-templates.walkthrough:
Tom Bradley teaches 4th grade and is tired of typing the same kinds of parent messages from scratch every week. He opens ChatGPT and fills GRADE with "4th grade" and lists his scenarios: "1) missing homework pattern (repeat), 2) positive recognition, 3) grade concern check-in, 4) unexcused absence follow-up."

ChatGPT returns four templates, each under 120 words. The missing homework one reads: "Hi [Parent Name], I wanted to reach out because [Student Name] hasn't turned in homework on [number] occasions this [week/month], most recently on [date]. I know things come up — could we do a quick call this week to figure out what's getting in the way?" Each concern-type template ends with a specific next step instead of just a complaint, and the recognition one is upbeat without needing an ask, matching its different purpose.

Tom notices the templates are written at email length, but he actually sends most parent messages through the school's text app, so he sends the follow-up asking ChatGPT to shorten each one to under 40 words for text messaging while keeping the placeholders. ChatGPT trims them down, cutting the missing-homework one to: "Hi [Parent Name] — [Student Name] has missed [number] homeworks this month, most recently [date]. Can we do a 10-minute call this week?"

Total time: about 7 minutes to get both the email-length and text-length versions. Tom saves both sets in a notes app so he can copy one, fill in the brackets with a real name and date, and send a personalized message in under a minute the next time an issue comes up, never sending a template with the placeholder brackets still showing.

placeholders.name: STANDARDS DOCUMENT NAME
placeholders.what: The exact file name of your standards document as you uploaded it into the Claude Project's knowledge — check the project's files list to see the precise name Claude is using. Getting this exact match matters because Claude cites sources by name, and a close-but-wrong name can cause it to search the wrong document.
examples: 7th_Grade_ELA_CCSS_Standards.pdf
NGSS_MS_Standards_2024.pdf
Algebra1_State_Standards_Master_List.docx

placeholders.name: X
placeholders.what: The current week number of your school year according to your own pacing guide, not the calendar week. Check the pacing guide document you uploaded to find which week you're on; a good value matches exactly what your pacing guide calls it, for example if your guide starts counting at week 1 in late August, use that same numbering.

variations.label: Mid-Unit Check
variations.whenToUse: Use this partway through a single unit rather than across the whole year, when you just want to confirm you've hit every standard tied to the unit you're currently teaching.
variations.prompt:
Using only the uploaded documents, answer: within [UNIT NAME], which of its tied standards from [STANDARDS DOCUMENT NAME] have I not yet covered, based on the lessons I've taught so far this unit?

For each uncovered standard:
- Cite the exact source document it comes from.
- Suggest which remaining lesson in this unit it best fits, based only on what's in the unit plan I uploaded.

If you are not sure whether a standard has been covered based on these documents, say so rather than guessing.

variations.label: Cross-Check Two Pacing Guides
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you co-teach or share a course with another teacher and want to confirm both sections are covering the same standards at the same pace.
variations.prompt:
Using only the uploaded documents, compare [PACING GUIDE 1 NAME] and [PACING GUIDE 2 NAME] as of week [X]. Which standards from [STANDARDS DOCUMENT NAME] does one section's pacing guide show as covered that the other doesn't?

For each mismatch:
- Cite the exact source document and week it appears in.
- Note which section, based on the pacing guide file name, is ahead on that standard.

If you're not sure whether a standard has been covered in either pacing guide based on these documents, say so rather than guessing.

variations.label: Generate a Catch-Up Plan
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you already know you're behind and want a concrete plan to fold missed standards into upcoming units, not just a list of gaps.
variations.prompt:
Using only the uploaded documents, identify which standards in [STANDARDS DOCUMENT NAME] I have not yet covered, based on my pacing guide as of week [X]. Then, using only my remaining unit plans, propose a catch-up plan for the rest of the year.

For each uncovered standard:
- Cite the exact source document it comes from.
- Tell me whether it can be folded into an already-planned upcoming unit (and which one) or needs a new standalone lesson.

Organize the result as a week-by-week list for the remaining weeks in my pacing guide. If you are not sure whether a standard has been covered, or whether it realistically fits into an existing unit, say so rather than guessing.

followUps.label: Ask for exact page or section citations
followUps.prompt: For each uncovered standard, give me the exact page number or section heading in the source document where I could double-check this myself, not just the file name.

followUps.label: Check for partially covered standards
followUps.prompt: Beyond standards with zero coverage, are there any standards that were only touched briefly or partially, based on what's in these documents? List those separately and explain what's missing to call them fully covered.

followUps.label: Turn the gaps into a week-by-week catch-up plan
followUps.prompt: Turn this list of uncovered standards into a week-by-week catch-up plan for the rest of my pacing guide, using only the upcoming units I've already uploaded. Tell me which standards fit into an existing unit and which need a new lesson.

followUps.label: Double-check its own uncertainty
followUps.prompt: Go back through your answer and tell me which of these conclusions you're most and least confident about, based only on the uploaded documents, so I know which ones to verify manually before I trust this list.

tch-i3-notebooklm-curriculum-knowledge-b.walkthrough:
Grace Okafor teaches 8th grade ELA and wants to know, six weeks before the state test, which standards she still hasn't taught. She opens Claude, creates a new Project, and uploads three files to its knowledge: her official standards document, named "8th_Grade_ELA_Standards.pdf," her pacing guide spreadsheet, and her unit plan documents for the semester so far. This upload step happens before any prompting — Claude needs the source files loaded into the project first so every answer it gives can be traced back to something she actually uploaded, not general knowledge about 8th grade standards.

Once the documents are in, she starts a new chat inside the project and pastes the prompt, filling STANDARDS DOCUMENT NAME with "8th_Grade_ELA_Standards.pdf" and X with "14," since it's week 14 of her pacing guide.

Claude lists five standards it can't find evidence of being covered, each naming its source, for example: "Standard RL.8.6, from 8th_Grade_ELA_Standards.pdf — no matching entry found in Pacing_Guide.xlsx or Unit_3_Plan.docx." For each, it suggests which upcoming unit fits best, based only on the unit plans she uploaded, and flags one standard as uncertain: "RI.8.7 may be partially covered in Unit 2 but the pacing guide doesn't specify which lesson — verify manually."

Grace wants more than a list, so she sends a follow-up asking Claude to turn the gaps into a week-by-week catch-up plan for her remaining seven weeks. It proposes folding two of the standards into her already-planned Unit 4 and flags that the other three need a dedicated new lesson.

Total time: about 12 minutes, most of it spent uploading files the first time. Every gap it named, she could check herself against the source document sitting right there in the project's knowledge.

placeholders.name: PASTE PROMPT
placeholders.what: The exact wording of your current assignment prompt or instructions, copied in full from your handout, LMS post, or slide, not a summary. The AI needs the real wording to spot exactly which parts are generic enough for an AI to fake without any of your class's specific context.
examples: Write a five-paragraph essay explaining three causes of the Cold War. Use your textbook and class notes. Minimum 750 words, due Friday.
Write a persuasive essay arguing for or against social media regulation for minors. Include at least two supporting reasons. 3-4 paragraphs, due next Monday.
Explain the process of photosynthesis in your own words, including the role of sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. One page, due next class.

placeholders.name: GRADE/SUBJECT
placeholders.what: The grade level and subject of the class this assignment is for, written together since both affect how AI-resistant an assignment needs to be. A good value is specific, like '11th grade, U.S. History'; a bad value is just 'high school.'
examples: 11th grade, U.S. History
9th grade Biology
7th grade English Language Arts

placeholders.name: DESCRIBE, e.g. "a generic five-paragraph essay with no reference to our specific class discussion or local case study"
placeholders.what: Your honest prediction of what a fully AI-ghostwritten answer to this exact assignment would look like — be specific about what it would be missing, like a local example, a specific text you read, a class debate, or a dataset, so the AI can design around exactly that gap. A vague answer like 'it would be bad' isn't useful here.
examples: a generic five-paragraph essay listing textbook causes with no reference to the primary source documents we analyzed in class or our Cold War simulation debate
a competent-sounding persuasive essay using generic talking points about screen time, with no mention of the survey data our class collected from the student body last week
a technically correct explanation of photosynthesis copied almost word-for-word from any biology textbook, with no reference to the plant-growth experiment we ran in class over the past two weeks

variations.label: Group Project Version
variations.whenToUse: Use this when the assignment is a group project rather than individual work, where you also need to make sure AI use doesn't let one student coast while others do the thinking.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me redesign a group assignment to be resistant to AI ghostwriting while still allowing students to use AI as a legitimate research or thinking tool.

ORIGINAL ASSIGNMENT: [PASTE PROMPT]
GRADE/SUBJECT: [GRADE/SUBJECT]
GROUP SIZE: [GROUP SIZE, e.g. "groups of 4"]
WHAT A FULLY AI-GHOSTWRITTEN SUBMISSION WOULD LOOK LIKE FOR THIS PROMPT: [DESCRIBE, e.g. "a generic five-paragraph essay with no reference to our specific class discussion or local case study"]

Give me:
1. A redesigned version of the assignment that requires evidence a generic AI response can't produce on its own, and that also makes each individual group member's contribution visible and separately assessable.
2. 2-3 checkpoint deliverables spaced across the timeline, at least one of which is an individual (not group) checkpoint, so I can see each student's own thinking, not just the group's final product.
3. A short, plain-language 'how you may use AI on this assignment' policy for students, with specific examples of allowed use and disallowed use, including how it applies differently to individual versus group portions.
4. A 15-minute lesson plan teaching students the difference between using AI to think and using AI to skip thinking, with one in-class discussion question about group accountability specifically.

Base this only on the assignment and context I gave you — don't invent facts about my school's policies.

variations.label: STEM Lab / Problem Set Version
variations.whenToUse: Use this for a math or science assignment where the ghostwriting risk is showing work or using a specific dataset, not writing prose.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me redesign a math or science assignment to be resistant to AI ghostwriting while still allowing students to use AI as a legitimate tool for checking work or getting unstuck.

ORIGINAL ASSIGNMENT: [PASTE PROMPT]
GRADE/SUBJECT: [GRADE/SUBJECT]
WHAT A FULLY AI-GENERATED SUBMISSION WOULD LOOK LIKE FOR THIS PROMPT: [DESCRIBE, e.g. "correct final answers with generic textbook-style work shown, no connection to the specific data our class collected in the lab"]

Give me:
1. A redesigned version of the assignment that requires students to use data, measurements, or numbers unique to our class (e.g. their own lab results, a dataset only our class has) so a generic AI answer can't match the specific numbers.
2. 2-3 checkpoint deliverables spaced across the timeline (e.g. raw data recorded in class, a first attempt at the calculation, a final write-up with an explanation of one error they caught and fixed) that make the student's own process visible.
3. A short, plain-language 'how you may use AI on this assignment' policy for students, with specific examples of allowed use (e.g. asking AI to explain a formula, checking a calculation) and disallowed use (e.g. having AI solve the problem from the data).
4. A 15-minute lesson plan teaching students the difference between using AI to check their thinking and using AI to skip the thinking, with one in-class discussion question specific to math/science work.

Base this only on the assignment and context I gave you — don't invent facts about my school's policies.

variations.label: Whole-Department Policy Version
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you want to build a consistent AI-use policy and assignment-design checklist across an entire department or grade team, not just redesign one assignment.
variations.prompt:
You are helping my department build a consistent approach to AI-resistant assignment design and a shared AI-use policy, starting from one example assignment.

EXAMPLE ASSIGNMENT: [PASTE PROMPT]
GRADE/SUBJECT: [GRADE/SUBJECT]
WHAT A FULLY AI-GHOSTWRITTEN SUBMISSION WOULD LOOK LIKE FOR THIS PROMPT: [DESCRIBE, e.g. "a generic five-paragraph essay with no reference to our specific class discussion or local case study"]
OTHER ASSIGNMENT TYPES OUR DEPARTMENT COMMONLY USES: [ASSIGNMENT TYPES, e.g. "essays, lab reports, reading responses, presentations"]

Give me:
1. A redesigned version of the example assignment that requires evidence a generic AI response can't produce on its own.
2. A general checklist (5-7 items) any teacher in the department can use to check whether one of their own assignments is AI-ghostwriting-resistant, based on the pattern in the redesigned example.
3. A short, plain-language 'how you may use AI on assignments' policy written generally enough to apply across the assignment types I listed, with specific examples of allowed and disallowed use for each type.
4. A 15-minute lesson plan teaching students the difference between using AI to think and using AI to skip thinking, with one in-class discussion question, that any teacher in the department could run as-is.

Base this only on the assignment and context I gave you — don't invent facts about my school's policies or assume department agreement that hasn't happened yet.

followUps.label: Make the AI-use policy more specific
followUps.prompt: The AI-use policy still feels a little abstract. Rewrite the allowed and disallowed lists with 4-5 concrete examples each, specific to this assignment, like 'allowed: asking AI to explain what an annotated bibliography is' and 'disallowed: pasting the checkpoint prompt into AI and submitting its output.'

followUps.label: Fit the checkpoints to a shorter timeline
followUps.prompt: I only have two weeks for this assignment, not the full timeline you assumed. Compress the checkpoints to fit two weeks and tell me which one is safe to combine with another if I'm short on class time.

followUps.label: Write the discussion question script
followUps.prompt: Write out the discussion question as an actual script I can read to the class, including one example of a strong student response and one example of a weak one, so I know what to listen for.

followUps.label: Check it isn't assuming resources I don't have
followUps.prompt: Reread the redesigned assignment and checkpoints and flag anything that assumes access I don't actually have — like a specific dataset, guest interview, or technology — so I can confirm what's realistic before I hand this out.

tch-a1-ai-resilient-assignments-literacy.walkthrough:
Jordan Kessler teaches 11th grade U.S. History and is worried his current essay prompt on the causes of the Cold War is too easy for AI to ghostwrite convincingly, since it's a generic "explain three causes" essay any AI could answer without knowing anything about his class. He opens Claude, pastes his original assignment into PASTE PROMPT, sets GRADE/SUBJECT to "11th grade, U.S. History," and describes the ghostwriting risk in DESCRIBE: "a generic five-paragraph essay listing textbook causes with no reference to the primary source documents we analyzed in class or our Cold War simulation debate."

Claude returns a redesigned assignment requiring students to reference two specific primary sources distributed in class and cite a moment from the in-class debate simulation by name. It proposes three checkpoints: a one-paragraph topic proposal naming which primary source they'll center the essay on, an annotated outline due a week later, and a final draft submitted with visible revision history using Google Docs version history. It writes a plain-language AI policy allowing brainstorming and grammar checks but disallowing generating full paragraphs, with examples of each. It also includes a 15-minute lesson with a discussion question: "If you asked an AI to write this essay right now, what would it get wrong about our class specifically?"

Jordan worries the discussion question is a little abstract for his class, so he sends the follow-up asking Claude to write it out as an actual script with a strong and a weak example response. Claude rewrites it as a short script he can read aloud, with both examples included.

Total time: about 13 minutes. Jordan now has a redesigned assignment, a policy he can paste into his syllabus, and a discussion activity ready for Monday.

placeholders.name: TOPIC
placeholders.what: The exact concept, theorem, process, or skill you're trying to learn — not the whole course, just one specific thing. You can find it on your syllabus, the assignment sheet, or the textbook's table of contents. A good value is narrow enough to actually check understanding of (e.g. 'oxidative phosphorylation'); a bad value is a whole course name like 'biology', which is too broad for the tutor to target questions.
examples: the Krebs cycle and where each stage happens in the cell
linear regression, specifically what R-squared measures
Newton's second law and drawing free-body diagrams

placeholders.name: CLASS/EXAM
placeholders.what: The course, level, or exam this topic is for — it tells the tutor how deep and technical to go. Pull this from your syllabus, course code, or the name printed on your study guide. A good value names the specific course and, if relevant, the exact test ('AP Chemistry, unit 4 test'); a bad value is vague, like 'school.'
examples: AP Biology, unit 3 test next Thursday
Intro Macroeconomics (ECON 201), midterm 2
AP Physics 1, in-class quiz on Friday

placeholders.name: YOUR ATTEMPT AT EXPLAINING IT
placeholders.what: Your own honest explanation of the topic right now, in plain language, written from memory before you check any notes or search anything. This is the raw material the tutor uses to find exactly what you're missing, so it needs to be genuinely yours — copying a definition from your textbook defeats the purpose. It's fine, even useful, if it's partly wrong or you trail off where you get unsure.
examples: Cellular respiration is how cells make energy from food. Glucose gets broken down and it makes ATP. I think it happens in the mitochondria. There's a step called glycolysis that happens first, outside the mitochondria I think, and it splits glucose into two smaller molecules. After that I'm fuzzy on what happens — I know oxygen is involved somewhere and CO2 comes out at the end.

Supply and demand means that when a product gets more popular, the price goes up because more people want it. If a company makes too much of something nobody wants, they have to lower the price to sell it. I think equilibrium is when the price stops changing because supply and demand are equal, but I'm not sure how to find that point on a graph or what shifts the curves versus moves along them.

Newton's second law is F=ma, force equals mass times acceleration. So heavier things need more force to move the same amount. I know you use free-body diagrams to show all the forces on an object but I always mix up which forces to include, and I don't really get why acceleration is zero when things are moving at a constant speed.

variations.label: Quick pre-class check-in
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you only have 5-10 minutes before class or a quiz and just need to know if you're missing something obvious, not a full deep-dive session.
variations.prompt:
I'm about to walk into [CLASS/EXAM] and want a 5-minute Socratic check on [TOPIC] before I go in.

Rules: don't explain anything up front. Ask me one question to test whether I actually understand [TOPIC]. If I get it wrong, tell me why and ask one more question — max 2 rounds total, then give me a one-line verdict: 'ready' or 'review this specific part before class.'

What I think I know:
[YOUR ATTEMPT AT EXPLAINING IT]

Go straight to your first question.

variations.label: Peer-teaching mode
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you want deeper active recall by having Claude play a confused classmate you have to teach, which forces you to produce the explanation instead of just answering questions.
variations.prompt:
I'm learning [TOPIC] for [CLASS/EXAM]. Instead of quizzing me directly, play the role of a classmate who is confused about [TOPIC] and needs me to teach it to them.

Rules:
- Ask me genuinely confused-student questions, including ones that expose gaps in my explanation.
- If my explanation to you is wrong or unclear, react the way a real confused student would (say you're more confused, or ask a follow-up that shows the gap) rather than telling me directly I'm wrong.
- Don't break character to explain the concept yourself unless I explicitly ask you to step out of the role and just tell me.

Here's how I'd start explaining it to you:
[YOUR ATTEMPT AT EXPLAINING IT]

Respond in character as the confused classmate.

variations.label: Full pre-exam audit across multiple topics
variations.whenToUse: Use this a few days before an exam when you need the tutor to sweep across everything on the exam, not just one concept, and tell you which topics need this Socratic treatment most.
variations.prompt:
I have an exam on [CLASS/EXAM] covering multiple topics. I want you to Socratically audit my understanding across all of them, not just one.

Topics to cover: [TOPIC]

Rules: go topic by topic. For each one, ask me to explain it first before you say anything. Tell me what's right and wrong, ask one guiding question if something's off, then move to the next topic — don't give full explanations unless I ask. At the end, rank the topics from strongest to weakest based on how the audit went.

Start with the first topic and ask me to explain it.

followUps.label: Ask for the smallest possible hint
followUps.prompt: I'm stuck — give me the smallest hint you can, just enough to get me unstuck, not the answer or the reasoning.

followUps.label: Confirm real understanding, not just repeating you
followUps.prompt: Now quiz me on this same topic a different way — change the example or angle — so I can prove I actually understand it and I'm not just repeating your explanation back.

followUps.label: Tutor gave away too much
followUps.prompt: That was too much of the answer. Go back to asking me guiding questions instead of explaining — I want to work it out myself.

followUps.label: Connect to the bigger picture
followUps.prompt: Now ask me a question that connects this topic to how it might show up in a harder or combined exam question, not just in isolation.

stu-b1-ai-tutor-without-cheating.walkthrough:
Priya has an AP Biology unit test on cellular respiration in four days. She opens Claude, pastes the lesson's prompt, and fills in the brackets: TOPIC becomes 'cellular respiration, especially the electron transport chain,' CLASS/EXAM becomes 'AP Biology, unit 4 test Thursday,' and for YOUR ATTEMPT AT EXPLAINING IT she writes three sentences from memory, admitting she isn't sure why oxygen is needed at the end of the chain.

Claude's first reply doesn't explain anything. It tells her she's right that glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, but flags that she's mixed up where the electron transport chain occurs (she said mitochondrial matrix; it's actually the inner mitochondrial membrane), and asks: 'What do you think would happen to the electron transport chain if there were no oxygen available at all?'

Priya guesses wrong — she says the cell would just slow down. Claude tells her that's not quite right and why, then asks a narrower question about where the electrons would back up. She's stuck, so she sends the first follow-up: 'I'm stuck — give me the smallest hint you can.' Claude gives one sentence about electron carriers filling up, not the full mechanism. That's enough — Priya works out that without oxygen to accept the final electrons, the whole chain backs up and stops.

She asks for the full explanation, then Claude asks her to explain it back in her own words, which she does, correctly this time. Before closing, she sends the peer-teaching-style follow-up asking Claude to quiz her from a different angle, to make sure she isn't just repeating the last answer back.

The whole session takes about 15 minutes. Priya ends it with a written explanation she generated herself, not one she copied — which is what she actually needs in order to remember it on Thursday.

variations.label: Fast chapter recap
variations.whenToUse: Use when you just need a quick refresher on a short reading before class discussion and don't need full self-check questions.
variations.prompt: Using only the uploaded document, give me a fast recap: one paragraph (5-6 sentences) summarizing the whole reading, then a bullet list of the 5 most important terms with one-sentence definitions taken directly from the text. Skip the self-check questions this time — I just need the recap. Do not add anything that isn't in the document.

variations.label: Seminar discussion prep
variations.whenToUse: Use before a class discussion or seminar where you need discussion questions and points to raise, not just quiz yourself.
variations.prompt:
Using only the uploaded document, do the following:
1. Summarize the reading section by section, 2-3 sentences per section, using the document's own headings.
2. List the 3 most debatable or contestable claims the author makes, each with the sentence or passage it comes from.
3. Write 4 discussion questions I could raise in seminar that engage with those debatable claims, not just factual recall.
4. For everything above, stay traceable to the source document only — no outside context.

variations.label: Multi-document synthesis
variations.whenToUse: Use when you've uploaded more than one reading (e.g. two articles assigned for the same week) and need to see where they agree, disagree, or build on each other, grounded in both texts.
variations.prompt:
Using only the uploaded documents (both of them), do the following:
1. Summarize each document separately, section by section, 2-3 sentences per section.
2. Identify 3 points where the two documents agree, and 3 points where they disagree or emphasize different things, citing which document each point comes from.
3. Write 4 self-check questions that require comparing both documents to answer, not just recalling one.
4. Stay traceable to the two uploaded documents only — do not add outside context.

followUps.label: Check for unsupported claims
followUps.prompt: Go back through your summary and self-check questions and flag anything that isn't directly supported by the uploaded document — if you added outside knowledge anywhere, tell me exactly where.

followUps.label: Make quiz questions harder
followUps.prompt: The 'explain why/how' questions were too easy. Rewrite them so they require connecting two different sections of the reading, not just restating one paragraph.

followUps.label: Clarify a confusing section
followUps.prompt: Ask me which section of the reading I'm still confused about, then explain just that section in plainer language, using only the document, with a concrete example if there is one.

followUps.label: Convert to flashcards
followUps.prompt: Turn the 5 key terms and their definitions into a flashcard format: term on one line, definition on the next, so I can copy them into a flashcard app.

stu-b2-summarize-question-readings.walkthrough:
Marcus has a 22-page reading on the origins of the Cold War due for his history seminar tomorrow. He opens Claude, starts a new chat, and uploads the PDF his professor posted using the attachment button. Once it finishes processing, he pastes the lesson's prompt into the chat box exactly as written — no edits needed since there are no placeholders to fill in.

Claude replies with a section-by-section summary using the reading's own subheadings ('Origins of Mutual Suspicion,' 'The Truman Doctrine,' 'Containment in Practice'), each two to three sentences. Below that: five key terms — containment, Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, iron curtain, and satellite state — each with a one-sentence definition quoted from the text. Then six self-check questions: three factual ('What year was the Truman Doctrine announced?') and three explain-why ('Why did containment require both military and economic tools, according to the reading?').

Marcus notices one question mentions NATO, but NATO isn't actually named anywhere in his reading — it must have pulled that from general knowledge instead of the document. He sends the follow-up asking Claude to flag anything not directly supported by the source. It re-checks, admits that question wasn't grounded in the text, replaces it with one about the Marshall Plan instead, and quotes the exact sentence the replacement question comes from.

Marcus quizzes himself using the six questions before closing his laptop, answering them on his own first rather than just reading the key — the point is checking his own understanding, not producing something to hand in. The whole thing takes about 12 minutes, and because he can check every claim against the actual PDF, he trusts the summary enough to actually study from it instead of re-reading all 22 pages the night before class.

placeholders.name: SUBJECT/TOPIC LIST
placeholders.what: The subject and/or the specific topics your exam will cover, as broad or as itemized as you currently know it — check your course syllabus, the exam study guide your teacher handed out, or the unit titles in your textbook. A good value lists the actual topic names ('cell division, genetics, and evolution'); a bad value is just the class name with no topics ('biology').
examples: Organic Chemistry: functional groups, reaction mechanisms, and stereochemistry
US History unit 5: the Progressive Era, WWI, and the 1920s
Statistics: hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, and p-values

placeholders.name: DATE
placeholders.what: The actual calendar date of your exam, taken directly from your syllabus or your school's portal — this is what the schedule counts backward from, so it needs to be the real date, not an estimate. This bracket appears twice in the prompt; use the same date both times. A good value is a specific date; a bad value is vague, like 'next week.'
examples: August 18, 2026
Friday, September 4
October 2, 2026

placeholders.name: X
placeholders.what: The number of days you actually have left before the exam, counted from today on a real calendar. Count it yourself rather than guessing, since the whole schedule depends on this number being accurate. A good value is a specific whole number; a bad value is a rough guess like 'a couple weeks.'

placeholders.name: Y
placeholders.what: How many minutes you can realistically study per day, based on your actual schedule (classes, work, sports) — not an ideal you won't hit most days. This bracket appears twice; use the same number both times so the schedule and the daily cap match. A bad value is an unrealistic number, like 240, that assumes a totally free schedule.

placeholders.name: PASTE NOTES OR TOPIC LIST
placeholders.what: Your actual class notes, a topic outline, or a bullet list of everything you've covered so far for this exam — copy-pasted from your notebook, slides, or study guide. This is the only material the practice questions and schedule will be built from, so the more complete and specific it is, the better the output; a bad value is a single vague line like 'chapter 5' with no actual content.
examples:
- Functional groups: alcohols (-OH), carboxylic acids (-COOH), amines (-NH2), esters
- SN1 vs SN2 reactions: SN1 is two steps, forms carbocation, works best with tertiary substrates; SN2 is one step, backside attack, works best with primary substrates
- E1 vs E2 elimination and Zaitsev's rule for the major product
- Stereochemistry: R/S configuration, assigning priority with CIP rules
- Chair conformations of cyclohexane, axial vs equatorial substituents
- Still confused on how to tell substitution from elimination based on the reagents given

- Progressive Era reforms: trust-busting, Pure Food and Drug Act, 19th Amendment
- Causes of WWI: alliances, militarism, assassination of Franz Ferdinand
- US entry into WWI: Zimmermann Telegram, unrestricted submarine warfare
- Treaty of Versailles and why the US Senate rejected it
- 1920s: Prohibition, the Scopes Trial, rise of consumer culture
- Need to review: causes of the Great Migration, still fuzzy on the dates

- Null vs alternative hypothesis, how to write H0 and Ha
- Type I vs Type II errors
- p-value: what it actually means (probability of data this extreme if H0 is true)
- Confidence intervals: how to interpret a 95% CI in words
- z-test vs t-test: when to use each
- Weak spot: calculating sample size needed for a given margin of error

variations.label: 1-2 day cram version
variations.whenToUse: Use when the exam is tomorrow or the day after and there's no time for spaced repetition — you need triage and one intensive pass, not a multi-day schedule.
variations.prompt:
I have an exam on [SUBJECT/TOPIC LIST] on [DATE] and only [X] days left — this is a cram situation, not a spaced-review situation.

My notes/topics: [PASTE NOTES OR TOPIC LIST]

1. Rank my topics from highest-yield (most likely to appear, or worth the most points) to lowest, based only on what's in my notes.
2. Generate 12 practice questions weighted toward the highest-yield topics, with an answer key that includes a 1-sentence reason for each answer.
3. Build an hour-by-hour schedule for the time remaining, capped at [Y] minutes per session, that front-loads the highest-yield topics and leaves the last block before the exam for my weakest topic only.

Do not add topics that aren't in my notes — ask me instead of assuming.

variations.label: Study group version
variations.whenToUse: Use when you're prepping with 2-3 classmates and want a shared plan that splits topics and a combined practice test you can quiz each other with.
variations.prompt:
My study group (3-4 people) has an exam on [SUBJECT/TOPIC LIST] on [DATE]. We have [X] days left and can meet for [Y] minutes per session.

Combined notes/topics from the group: [PASTE NOTES OR TOPIC LIST]

1. Split the topics into roughly equal chunks, one per group member, so each person can become the 'expert' who explains their chunk to the others.
2. Generate 15 practice questions covering all topics combined, with an answer key, that we can use to quiz each other.
3. Build a day-by-day schedule for our group sessions using spaced repetition, noting which member should lead each session's review.

Do not add topics that aren't in our combined notes — ask us instead of assuming.

variations.label: Cumulative final exam version
variations.whenToUse: Use for a final exam covering an entire semester's worth of material across multiple units, where the schedule needs to weight review toward older topics you're most likely to have forgotten.
variations.prompt:
I have a cumulative final exam on [SUBJECT/TOPIC LIST] on [DATE], covering the whole semester. I have [X] days left and can study [Y] minutes/day.

My notes/topics from the whole semester: [PASTE NOTES OR TOPIC LIST]

1. Generate 20 practice questions weighted toward earlier-semester topics, since those are the ones I'm most likely to have forgotten, with an answer key.
2. Build a day-by-day spaced review schedule that revisits early-semester topics more frequently than recent ones, capped at [Y] minutes per day.
3. Flag which early-semester topics look thinnest in my notes, since those are the highest-risk gaps for a cumulative exam.

Do not add topics that aren't in my notes — ask me instead of assuming.

followUps.label: Answer key too thin
followUps.prompt: For each answer in the key, add a 1-2 sentence explanation of why it's correct, not just the answer itself, so I can check my reasoning, not only my final answer.

followUps.label: Schedule doesn't fit a specific day
followUps.prompt: I actually have less time than planned on one of the days — rebuild the schedule assuming I only get 15 minutes that day and redistribute the rest across the remaining days without exceeding my daily limit.

followUps.label: More practice on weak topics
followUps.prompt: Generate 8 more practice questions focused only on the topics you flagged as weakest, with the answer key, and make them harder than the first set.

followUps.label: Double-check nothing was invented
followUps.prompt: Go back through the practice questions and schedule and confirm every topic came from my notes — if any question tests something not in what I gave you, tell me exactly which one and remove or replace it.

stu-b3-exam-prep-practice-spaced-review.walkthrough:
Elena has an Organic Chemistry exam in 6 days and roughly 60 minutes a day to study around her part-time job. She opens ChatGPT and pastes the lesson prompt, filling in SUBJECT/TOPIC LIST as 'functional groups, SN1/SN2 reactions, and stereochemistry,' DATE as the actual exam date from her syllabus, X as '6,' Y as '60,' and for PASTE NOTES OR TOPIC LIST she copies six bullet points straight from her notebook, including one line admitting she's shaky on telling substitution from elimination reactions.

ChatGPT responds with 15 practice questions (mostly multiple choice, a few short answer) and an answer key underneath. Then it lays out a day-by-day schedule: Day 1 covers functional groups and SN1/SN2 basics fresh; Day 3 briefly revisits functional groups (spaced repetition) while introducing stereochemistry; Day 5 mixes all three topics together as a timed mini-quiz; Day 6 is a light final review, capped at 60 minutes every day. It flags substitution-versus-elimination as her weakest area based on her own note, and asks whether the exam also covers addition reactions, since her notes never mentioned them.

Elena confirms addition reactions aren't on this exam, so nothing changes. She sends the follow-up asking for explanations behind each answer key entry, since a few multiple-choice answers left her wondering why the other options were wrong. ChatGPT adds a short reasoning line under each one.

Setting this up took about 10 minutes. Elena now has a printed schedule taped above her desk and a stack of practice questions she works through each day, catching herself forgetting the SN1/SN2 distinction on day 3 — exactly as the spaced schedule predicted she might.

placeholders.name: PASTE YOUR DRAFT
placeholders.what: The actual text of your own essay, paper, or assignment draft, copied in full or at least the section you want feedback on — pulled from your Google Doc, Word file, or wherever you're writing. It must be work you wrote yourself; pasting something you didn't write, or that another AI generated for you, defeats the entire point of this exercise and makes the feedback meaningless for your revision.
examples: In The Great Gatsby, Fitzgerald shows that the American Dream is corrupted by wealth. Gatsby wants to be with Daisy but he can't because of money and social class. The green light represents his hope. Nick is the narrator and he judges everyone but also seems to admire Gatsby. I think this shows that money can't buy happiness and that the 1920s were a time of moral decay. The parties Gatsby throws are really extravagant and show how much money he has.

Social media has a negative effect on teenagers' mental health because it causes them to compare themselves to others. Studies show that teens who use social media a lot report feeling more anxious. Instagram especially shows filtered photos that aren't real. Also, teens spend less time with friends in person because they are on their phones instead. This is a problem because in-person connection is important for mental health, and I think schools should teach kids about this in health class.

placeholders.name: PASTE PROMPT OR GOAL
placeholders.what: The actual assignment instructions from your teacher or professor (copy them from the syllabus, the assignment sheet, or the LMS/Canvas page), or, if there's no formal prompt, a one-sentence statement of what the piece is supposed to accomplish. This tells the AI what to measure your draft against — without it, feedback defaults to generic writing advice instead of whether you actually met the assignment.
examples: Write a 3-page literary analysis essay arguing a specific interpretation of a central theme in The Great Gatsby, using at least 3 textual quotations as evidence. Due Friday.
Argumentative essay, 1200 words: take a position on a current social issue and support it with at least two cited sources. Persuade a skeptical reader.
Personal narrative essay, 750 words, for the college common app — show growth or change through a specific experience, don't just tell the reader what you learned.

variations.label: Quick sentence-level pass
variations.whenToUse: Use when your ideas and structure are already solid and you just want a fast check on clarity and awkward sentences before submitting, not a full argument review.
variations.prompt:
You are giving me feedback on my own writing, not rewriting it. Do not rewrite or generate replacement sentences at any point, even as an example — describe problems and ask questions instead.

My draft: [PASTE YOUR DRAFT]

Just focus on Clarity: point to specific sentences that are unclear, awkward, or overly complex (quote them exactly), explain what's unclear about them, and tell me what question a confused reader would ask at that point — but do not rewrite them for me. Limit it to the 5 sentences that would improve the piece the most if I fixed them.

variations.label: Deep structural review for a long paper
variations.whenToUse: Use for a longer research paper or thesis draft where you need feedback organized by section (intro, each body section, conclusion) rather than as one pass over the whole thing.
variations.prompt:
You are giving me feedback on my own writing, not rewriting it. Do not rewrite or generate replacement sentences or paragraphs at any point, even as an example — describe problems and ask questions instead.

My draft: [PASTE YOUR DRAFT]
Assignment/goal: [PASTE PROMPT OR GOAL]

Go section by section (introduction, each body section, conclusion). For each section, tell me: what its job is supposed to be in the overall argument, whether it actually does that job, and one specific question that would help me fix it if it doesn't. At the end, tell me if the sections are in the right order, and which one (if any) doesn't earn its place in the paper at all.

variations.label: Rubric-matched feedback
variations.whenToUse: Use when your teacher gave you a grading rubric and you want feedback organized around the actual rubric categories, so you know roughly how you'd score before you turn it in.
variations.prompt:
You are giving me feedback on my own writing, not rewriting it. Do not rewrite or generate replacement sentences or paragraphs at any point, even as an example — describe problems and ask questions instead.

My draft: [PASTE YOUR DRAFT]
Assignment/goal: [PASTE PROMPT OR GOAL]
Grading rubric (paste it exactly as given): [PASTE RUBRIC]

Go category by category through the rubric. For each category, tell me honestly where my draft currently sits against it, point to the specific evidence in my draft that supports that assessment, and ask me a question that would help me close the gap — do not rewrite anything for me. End with the single rubric category most likely to cost me points if I don't fix it.

followUps.label: Confirm nothing was rewritten
followUps.prompt: Double check your feedback above — did you rewrite or generate any replacement sentence anywhere, even as an example? If you did, point out exactly where so I can ignore it and fix it myself.

followUps.label: Want specific sentence references
followUps.prompt: Some of that feedback was too general. Go back through and for every issue you raised, quote the exact sentence from my draft it applies to.

followUps.label: Check my revision
followUps.prompt:
I revised the draft based on your feedback. Tell me which of the issues you raised are actually fixed now and which aren't — don't rewrite anything, just assess. Here's my revision:

(paste revised draft here)

followUps.label: Prioritize what matters most
followUps.prompt: If I only have 30 minutes to revise before this is due, which single issue from your feedback should I fix first, and why does it matter more than the others?

stu-i1-writing-feedback-not-ghostwriting.walkthrough:
Jordan is a college freshman with a literary analysis essay on The Great Gatsby due Friday. He's written a full first draft in Google Docs. He opens Claude, pastes the lesson's prompt, and fills in PASTE YOUR DRAFT with his actual three paragraphs (including the slightly generic line 'I think this shows that money can't buy happiness'), and PASTE PROMPT OR GOAL with the assignment sheet text his professor posted on Canvas: argue a specific interpretation using at least three quotations.

Claude's response is organized into the four categories from the prompt. Under Argument, it points out his thesis says wealth 'corrupts' the American Dream but his second paragraph mostly describes the parties without connecting them back to that claim, and asks: 'What specifically about the parties shows corruption, rather than just wealth?' Under Evidence, it notes he hasn't used a single direct quotation yet, which conflicts with the assignment's requirement of three. Under Clarity, it quotes his sentence about money and moral decay and explains that stacking two separate claims in one sentence makes it hard to tell which one he's actually arguing — but it does not rewrite the sentence for him. It ends by naming the two highest-impact fixes: add textual evidence, and narrow the thesis to one claim.

Jordan rewrites two sentences himself and adds a quotation about the green light. Unsure if he fixed the clarity issue, he sends the third follow-up, pasting his revision and asking Claude to assess it without rewriting anything. Claude confirms the thesis is now narrower but says the new quotation still needs one more sentence explaining how it supports his point.

Total time: about 20 minutes, and every sentence in the final essay is still Jordan's own writing.

placeholders.name: RESEARCH QUESTION / WORKING THESIS
placeholders.what: The specific question your paper is trying to answer, or the tentative argument (working thesis) you're currently planning to make — not the general topic. Pull this from your assignment prompt or the working thesis you already drafted with your professor or TA. A good value is answerable or arguable and specific; a bad value is a broad topic with no question attached, like 'social media.'
examples: Does heavy Instagram use in teenagers (ages 13-17) correlate with increased anxiety symptoms, and if so, why?
Working thesis: Remote work policies disproportionately benefit white-collar employees while widening inequality for hourly workers.
How did redlining in the 1930s-1950s shape present-day racial wealth gaps in US cities?

placeholders.name: e.g. "at least 3 peer-reviewed sources, published after 2015, APA citation style"
placeholders.what: The specific requirements your assignment gives for sources and citations — number of sources, how recent they need to be, whether they must be peer-reviewed, and which citation style to use. Copy these directly from your assignment sheet or rubric; don't guess, because getting this wrong (using MLA when APA is required, for example) costs easy points.
examples: at least 5 sources, minimum 3 peer-reviewed, published after 2018, MLA 9th edition citation style
4 sources total, at least 2 primary sources, no citation style specified but must include full bibliographic info
6-8 sources, all peer-reviewed journal articles, published within the last 10 years, APA 7th edition

variations.label: Open-access only version
variations.whenToUse: Use when your school library access is limited or you need sources you can actually read in full for free, not just abstracts behind a paywall.
variations.prompt:
I'm researching: [RESEARCH QUESTION / WORKING THESIS]
Requirements: [e.g. "at least 3 peer-reviewed sources, published after 2015, APA citation style"], and every source must be something I can actually read in full for free (open-access journals, university repositories, or publicly posted PDFs) — no paywalled-only sources.

1. Suggest 6-8 candidate sources that meet both the requirements and the open-access condition, with publication, author, year, and a real link where possible. Tell me clearly if you're not fully certain a source exists, is open-access, or if any detail is correct — I will verify every source myself before using it.
2. For each source, give a 1-sentence description of its likely angle based only on its title/abstract.

I will confirm access and read the actual sources myself before citing anything.

variations.label: Annotated bibliography format
variations.whenToUse: Use when your assignment specifically requires a formatted annotated bibliography (each source with a citation plus a paragraph of annotation) rather than a working source list.
variations.prompt:
I'm researching: [RESEARCH QUESTION / WORKING THESIS]
Requirements: [e.g. "at least 3 peer-reviewed sources, published after 2015, APA citation style"]

1. Suggest 6-8 candidate sources with full citation details, flagging clearly anywhere you're not fully certain a source exists or a detail is correct.
2. Format each as an annotated bibliography entry: full citation in the required style, followed by a short annotation (2-3 sentences) describing its likely argument/angle and how it might relate to my research question, based only on the title/abstract.

I will read the actual sources myself and correct or remove any entry before using it in my paper.

variations.label: Counter-argument sources
variations.whenToUse: Use once you already have supporting sources and need sources that challenge or complicate your thesis, so your paper can address counterarguments instead of ignoring them.
variations.prompt:
I'm researching: [RESEARCH QUESTION / WORKING THESIS] and I already have supporting sources for my main argument.
Requirements: [e.g. "at least 3 peer-reviewed sources, published after 2015, APA citation style"]

1. Suggest 4-6 candidate sources that specifically challenge, complicate, or offer a different angle on my working thesis, not ones that just support it. Flag clearly if you're not fully certain a source exists or a detail is correct.
2. For each one, give a 1-sentence description of the counterargument or complication it likely raises, based only on its title/abstract.

I will read the actual sources myself and verify before citing anything.

followUps.label: Verify a source before using it
followUps.prompt: For source #3 on your list, tell me again exactly how confident you are that it's real and that the details (author, year, journal) are accurate — I'm about to go look it up myself and want to know what to double check.

followUps.label: Only recent sources
followUps.prompt: Drop any source you suggested that's older than 5 years and replace it with a more recent one on the same angle, following the same rule — flag it clearly if you're not fully certain it exists.

followUps.label: Format the verified ones
followUps.prompt: I've now confirmed sources 1, 3, and 5 are real and I've read them. Format full citations for just those three in the citation style from my requirements, and don't touch the others.

followUps.label: Different angle needed
followUps.prompt: I already have enough sources on that angle. Suggest 4 more candidate sources that instead look at a different mechanism or effect related to my research question, with the same certainty flags as before.

stu-i2-research-papers-find-organize-syn.walkthrough:
Tasha is writing a psychology term paper and needs at least 3 peer-reviewed sources published after 2015, in APA style. She opens Gemini and pastes the lesson's prompt, filling RESEARCH QUESTION / WORKING THESIS with 'Does heavy Instagram use in teenagers correlate with increased anxiety symptoms, and if so, why?' and the requirements placeholder with 'at least 3 peer-reviewed sources, published after 2015, APA citation style.'

Gemini returns 7 candidate sources. For five of them it gives a full citation with what looks like a working link or DOI and states it's reasonably confident these are real. For two others, it explicitly flags: 'I'm not fully certain this exact article exists — the author and general topic are correct as far as I know, but please verify the title and journal before citing it.' For each source it adds one sentence on the likely angle, for example: 'This one likely argues social comparison, not screen time itself, is the real mechanism behind the anxiety link.'

Tasha opens her university library database and checks all 7. Two of the 'confident' ones check out immediately. One of the flagged ones turns out not to exist at all under that title — the journal is real but that specific article isn't. She sends the first follow-up on source #3, gets Gemini's honest reassessment, and decides to drop it rather than risk citing something fake.

Once she's confirmed 5 real sources by reading their actual abstracts, she sends the follow-up asking Gemini to format full APA citations for just those five. It does, and she pastes them straight into her working bibliography.

The whole process — searching, verifying, and organizing — takes about 25 minutes, versus the hour she usually spends blindly searching databases with no starting angle.

placeholders.name: SPECIFIC NARROW SKILL
placeholders.what: The one specific skill you're drilling, narrow enough that a single practice problem can target it — not a whole subject. Think in terms of what you'd tell a tutor you need to practice, like a specific programming construct, math technique, or grammar rule. A good value is narrow ('nested for-loops in Python'); a bad value is broad ('programming').
examples: nested for-loops in Python
SQL JOINs (INNER vs LEFT)
balancing chemical equations

placeholders.name: YOUR LEVEL, e.g. "can write a basic for-loop but struggle with nested loops"
placeholders.what: An honest, specific description of what you can currently do and exactly where you get stuck, written from your own recent experience — not a guess at what level you 'should' be. This calibrates the difficulty of the very first practice problem, so vague answers like 'beginner' produce a badly-calibrated problem. A good value names both what works and exactly where it breaks.
examples: can write a basic for-loop that prints numbers 1-10, but when I try to nest one loop inside another for a multiplication table, I lose track of which variable belongs to which loop
comfortable with INNER JOIN but I don't understand when a LEFT JOIN gives different results or why NULLs show up
can balance equations with simple molecules like H2O but get stuck when there are polyatomic ions like sulfate on both sides

placeholders.name: PASTE YOUR ATTEMPT WHEN READY — leave blank for now and just send the first problem
placeholders.what: Once you receive the practice problem, this is where you paste your actual attempt at solving it — your code, your worked-out math, or your written answer, exactly as you produced it, not cleaned up. Leave this blank on your very first message so the AI sends you a problem first; only fill it in on your next message after you've genuinely tried.
examples: SELECT customers.name, orders.total FROM customers LEFT JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id WHERE orders.total > 100; -- I expected this to include customers with no orders too but they're missing from the results
Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + NaCl -- I know I need to balance the Na and Cl but I'm not sure if I balance the sulfate as one unit or break it into S and O separately

variations.label: Interview-style timed practice
variations.whenToUse: Use when you're prepping for a coding interview or timed exam and want problems delivered under time pressure with a harder ramp-up, closer to real test conditions.
variations.prompt:
I'm practicing [SPECIFIC NARROW SKILL] for a technical interview, currently at [YOUR LEVEL, e.g. "can write a basic for-loop but struggle with nested loops"].

Give me ONE problem at interview difficulty for this skill, and tell me a realistic time limit for it before you give it to me. Do not give me the solution yet.

After I submit my attempt within the time limit:
- Tell me specifically what's correct and what's wrong, referencing my actual attempt.
- Comment on whether I'd have passed a real interview on this answer, and why.
- Only show a full corrected solution if I get it wrong twice or explicitly ask.
- If I pass, give me the next problem, one step harder, with a new time limit.

My attempt: [PASTE YOUR ATTEMPT WHEN READY — leave blank for now and just send the first problem]

variations.label: Non-coding technical skill (e.g. spreadsheet formulas)
variations.whenToUse: Use this same loop for a non-programming technical skill, like Excel formulas or statistical calculations, where the 'attempt' is a formula or worked calculation instead of code.
variations.prompt:
I'm practicing [SPECIFIC NARROW SKILL], currently at [YOUR LEVEL, e.g. "can write a basic for-loop but struggle with nested loops"].

Diego works through four problems in this loop over about 25 minutes, with the last one taking him only one attempt — a visible sign he closed the gap he started with.
